title: Euclid’s view of irregular galaxy NGC 6822
caption: The irregular dwarf galaxy NGC 6822, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: NGC 6822 · constellation Sagittarius · about 1.6 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: One of Euclid’s first five full-color images (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A loose, shapeless crowd of stars fills the middle of this Euclid image. It is NGC 6822, an irregular dwarf galaxy just 1.6 million light-years from Earth in Sagittarius, a near neighbor by cosmic standards. It was the first irregular dwarf galaxy Euclid observed.

Galaxies in the early universe mostly weren’t the tidy spirals of textbook pictures. They tended to be small and irregular, and they were the building blocks of larger galaxies like our own. A few of these small galaxies survive nearby, which makes NGC 6822 a window into how galaxies grew.

To build its 3D map of the universe, Euclid will observe light from galaxies out to 10 billion light-years away. This view took about an hour. In its colors, hot stars look white-blue, glowing hydrogen appears blue, and dusty, gas-rich regions turn red.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (41 × 41 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 1.6 million light-years, the frame spans roughly 19,000 × 19,000 light-years. Its light set out about 1.6 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science. Distant galaxies far behind NGC 6822 show up as small red smudges.
alt: A loose, irregular cloud of faint stars among bright foreground stars with six-pointed spikes.
